title: SK Hynix commits $28B to buy back and cancel treasury shares — largest ever in Korea
subtitle: The memory-chip maker will retire up to 24 million shares between August 20 and November 19 and raised its 2025–2027 shareholder-return floor to more than 50% of free cash flow.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: SK Hynix filed a 6-K with the SEC on August 19 disclosing a plan to buy back and cancel up to 24 million treasury shares — roughly 40 trillion won, or about $28.6 billion — between August 20 and November 19. It is the largest treasury-share cancellation ever announced by a listed South Korean company. The company also raised its 2025–2027 shareholder-return target from 'up to 50%' of cumulative free cash flow to 'more than 50%.'

The move follows a nearly 10% single-day drop in the stock earlier in the week after investors questioned the durability of U.S. hyperscaler AI capex. SK Hynix is the dominant supplier of the high-bandwidth memory that sits next to Nvidia's Blackwell accelerators, and its cash flow has hit historic highs as HBM supply has stayed tight and prices firm. Retiring shares — rather than a dividend or a fresh capex commitment — signals the board thinks the current cash pile is durable enough to reward shareholders directly.

The broader arc matters. Memory suppliers were commodity roadkill for most of the 2010s; the AI training and inference cycle has repositioned them as gatekeepers to compute. Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix have all raised HBM capex through 2026, and the Korean player has been the first to convert that windfall into a shareholder-return package this large. It also puts a floor under the debate over whether AI-memory demand is real or a stocking bubble — a company only cancels this much stock when its finance team believes free cash flow is not a one-year event.

For learners, this is the plumbing of the AI economy showing through the floorboards. The models people talk about — Astra, Gemini 3.7, Qwen — all run on stacks of HBM sitting next to GPUs. When one of the two firms in the world that make that memory retires $28 billion of its own stock, that is a stronger signal about the shape of AI demand than any product launch. Follow the memory suppliers if you want an early read on which way the compute cycle is moving.
